name: Cimetidine for acne

lead: Cimetidine is an H2 blocker developed in the 1970s for ulcers and heartburn. Because it can weakly block androgen receptors at high doses, it was tried off-label for acne, aiming at less oil and fewer androgen-driven breakouts.

The research is small and dated: a 1979 Lancet report, a 1980 Lancet paper titled "Lack of effect of cimetidine in acne", and a 1986 German pilot study of a 2% topical lotion in ten patients that reported generally good results, with comedones responding best. Wikipedia describes its androgen-blocking effect as too weak to help much with acne, and no modern trials were found.

paras: It was used by mouth or as a topical lotion in those studies. Acne is an off-label use, and the drug is more commonly encountered for stomach acid.
Usually mild effects such as diarrhea and dizziness; gynecomastia and sexual dysfunction at higher doses; it inhibits liver enzymes, can raise estrogen levels and has many drug interactions.

angle.text: Cimetidine, a stomach-acid drug, was tried off-label for acne decades ago because of its weak antiandrogen activity, aiming at less oil and fewer breakouts. It was studied by mouth and as a lotion in small, dated studies.

lead: Cimetidine is a histamine H2 receptor antagonist developed at Smith, Kline & French in the 1970s to reduce stomach acid, and it is sold in many countries for ulcers and heartburn.[1] Because it has a weak ability to block androgen receptors at high doses, it has occasionally been tried as an off-label treatment for acne, both by mouth and as a topical lotion.[1]

The published evidence on acne is small and dated. A 1979 Lancet report and a 1980 Lancet paper titled "Lack of effect of cimetidine in acne" are among the early items,[2][3] and a 1986 German-language pilot study of a 2% topical lotion in ten patients reported generally good clinical results, with comedones responding best and pustules hardly reduced.[4] Wikipedia describes its androgen-blocking effect as too weak to help much with acne or hirsutism, and the drug is not recommended for those uses.[1]
infobox: Oral; topical lotion tested in a small study

paras: The established uses of cimetidine are duodenal and gastric ulcers, gastroesophageal reflux disease and heartburn.[1] Use in acne is off-label and is not part of standard acne treatment.[1]

Cimetidine blocks H2 receptors in the stomach and also inhibits several cytochrome P450 enzymes, which accounts for many drug interactions.[1] It weakly antagonizes the androgen receptor, but only at high doses, which is the basis of the proposal that it could reduce androgen-driven sebum and acne.[1] It can also raise estrogen levels by inhibiting estradiol metabolism.[1]

Wikipedia reports a Kd of 42 nM for the H2 receptor and describes cimetidine as a moderate, non-selective inhibitor of CYP1A2, CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 through binding to heme iron, which explains many drug interactions [1]. Its androgen receptor affinity is described as very low, about 0.00084 percent of that of metribolone, and it can reduce estradiol 2-hydroxylation, which may raise estrogen levels [1].

Oral bioavailability is 60 to 70 percent with onset in about 30 minutes, peak levels at 1 to 3 hours, protein binding of 13 to 25 percent, 56 to 85 percent excreted unchanged in urine, and an elimination half-life of about 123 minutes with a duration of action of 4 to 8 hours [1].

Cimetidine was developed at Smith, Kline & French Laboratories in Welwyn Garden City by James W. Black, C. Robin Ganellin and colleagues, and is described as one of the first drugs made through rational drug design: the program started from the structure of histamine, passed through burimamide and metiamide (dropped over kidney toxicity and agranulocytosis), and arrived at cimetidine [1]. It was synthesised in 1972, passed toxicology testing by 1973, was approved in the UK in 1976 and first marketed in the US in August 1977, and by 1979 Tagamet was sold in over 100 countries and became the first drug to pass $1 billion in annual sales [1]. Proton pump inhibitors have largely replaced it for ulcers, though it remains available over the counter for heartburn in many countries [1].
The acne reports followed soon after the drug's launch: a 1979 Lancet item and a 1980 Lancet paper on lack of effect appear within three years of the US launch [2][3].

Published human data on acne are sparse and old. Lancet carried a 1979 item titled "Cimetidine in acne" and a 1980 paper titled "Lack of effect of cimetidine in acne."[2][3] In a 1986 pilot study in the Zeitschrift fur Hautkrankheiten, ten patients with papulopustular and comedonal acne applied a 2% cimetidine lotion twice daily for an average of 13 weeks; the authors reported generally good clinical success, best for comedones and then papules, little reduction of pustules, and no significant reduction in sebum excretion rate.[4] The study was uncontrolled and small.

Common effects of oral cimetidine are usually mild and include diarrhea, rash, dizziness, fatigue and constipation.[1] Gynecomastia is rare at usual doses but more likely at high doses, and sexual dysfunction and reduced sperm count have been reported.[1] Liver enzyme elevations are common but usually transient.[1]

Gynecomastia incidence is under 1 percent at ulcer-treatment doses and higher at the high doses used for Zollinger-Ellison syndrome; one UK database study put the relative risk at 7.2, with the highest risk 7 to 12 months after starting [1].

Cimetidine is prescription-only in Australia (Schedule 4) and the UK, and in the US it is prescription-only or over the counter depending on formulation [1]. Wikipedia states that cimetidine has shown minimal effectiveness for acne, hirsutism and hyperandrogenism and that use for these conditions is not recommended; in warts, some early evidence of benefit was not confirmed in double-blind trials, which found it no better than placebo [1].
